title: The Juggling Act of Being a Manager
excerpt: This article explores the balancing act of managing down and managing up, and why focusing on your responsibilities, supporting your team and taking ownership can ultimately make managing upwards much easier.
content:
One of the things nobody tells you when you become a manager is that you're suddenly managing in two directions.

There's the obvious part: the people who work for you. You have 1:1s, give feedback, help people develop, deal with performance issues and try to create an environment where people can do their best work. Then there's your own manager.

At times those two responsibilities pull in completely different directions. Your team might want one thing while your manager wants another. You might understand why a decision was made at a senior level and know your team won't be happy about it. Or you might be pushing something forward for your team while priorities keep arriving from above. That's a big part of why management can feel like such a juggling act.

## Suddenly, you're in the middle

As an individual contributor, things can feel relatively straightforward. There are competing priorities and other people to consider, of course, but you're ultimately responsible for your own work, your own goals and your own contribution.

Becoming a manager changes that. You're now responsible for a group of people, and your team, your manager, other teams and the wider business all have expectations of you. You've become the connection between the people doing the work and the people setting the direction.

You can't always keep all of them happy. Sometimes your manager will want something your team doesn't. Sometimes your team will need something that isn't a priority for your manager. Sometimes you'll have to deliver a message to your team that you don't agree with yourself. At those moments, management feels less like a position of authority and more like keeping a lot of plates spinning at once.

## Managing down

The people you manage are probably the part of the job you think about most, and rightly so. You want them to succeed and enjoy their work. You want to help them develop, remove obstacles, give them clarity and make sure they have the support they need.

That doesn't mean keeping everyone happy. Sometimes you have to give difficult feedback or challenge someone's behaviour. Sometimes you have to tell someone that what they want isn't possible right now, or make a decision you know won't be popular.

Supporting your team and always giving your team what they want are two different things. Your responsibility is to help them succeed, and that can't mean shielding them from every difficult decision or uncomfortable conversation. Avoiding those conversations often does more harm than good. If someone isn't performing as they should, they need to know. If there's a problem in the team, it needs addressing. If priorities have changed, people need to understand why.

Being a good manager means being there for your people, and it also means being prepared to tell them things they might not want to hear.

## And then there's managing up

While you're doing all that, you've also got your own manager to think about. They have their own priorities, deadlines and pressures. They need information from you, and they need confidence that the things you're responsible for are under control.

Managing up is a real skill. You need to understand what your manager cares about and communicate clearly with them. You need to raise problems before they become surprises, and push back with your reasoning when you disagree.

All of that matters, but I think there's a danger in becoming too focused on it. I've seen people spend a huge amount of energy working out what their manager wants to hear: how to present something, how a decision might be perceived, how to make sure they're seen in the right way. Some of that is sensible, because understanding your manager is part of the job. Done constantly, though, it becomes exhausting.

## Maybe the best way to manage up is to manage down well

My own thinking on this has changed over time.

I used to think managing up was something you had to work at all the time, and to some extent you do. Your manager needs to know what's happening, and you need to understand the wider context your team is working in.

But I've increasingly come to believe that the best way to manage up is to do your own job well. Know what you're responsible for. Understand what your team needs. Deliver what you've committed to, raise problems early, don't hide mistakes, and above all, take ownership.

Do that consistently and a lot of the managing-up problem takes care of itself. Your manager doesn't have to chase you for updates, because they know you'll keep them informed. They don't have to worry about your team, because they trust you to deal with problems. And when you do disagree with something, your opinion carries more weight because you've built a reputation for being thoughtful and reliable. Once that trust is there, you don't need to spend your life managing your manager.

## Being the connection

That position in the middle is, I think, what makes management difficult. Information has to travel in both directions, and part of your job is making sure it does.

You need to understand what the leadership team is trying to achieve and turn that into something your team can understand and work towards. You also need to understand what's really happening in your team and make sure the people above you see the reality on the ground.

Sometimes that means translating, and sometimes it means challenging. Sometimes it means protecting your team from unnecessary noise, or explaining a decision to them even when you know they won't like it. You're standing in the middle, trying to help both sides understand each other while still looking after the responsibilities you've been given.

## You can't control everything

This is where the juggling analogy earns its place. You can't control everything above you or everything below you. There will always be competing priorities, difficult decisions and things outside your control.

What you *can* control is how you respond. You can make sure your team knows what's expected of them, give people honest feedback and support their development. You can raise problems early, take responsibility when things go wrong and give others the credit when things go right. And you can make sure your own manager isn't left wondering what's happening.

For me, that's the balance. Managing up shouldn't be ignored, but it shouldn't become the thing you spend most of your energy on either. If you look after your team and your own responsibilities, both your manager and your team know they can trust you, and you know you're doing the job you were trusted to do.

There will always be competing demands, difficult conversations and situations where somebody doesn't get what they want. The skill is balancing all of it without losing sight of what you're there to do. Feeling stuck in the middle doesn't mean something has gone wrong. The middle is where a manager is meant to be.
